system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

Here are examples of what I expect:

--- Example 1 ---
Original Medical Report:
Patient Name: Michael Smith | Age/Sex: 32/M | Admission: 02/03/2026 | Discharge: 05/03/2026
C/O: Loose stools, vomiting, and abdominal cramps for 3 days.
History: Multiple episodes of watery diarrhea with nausea, repeated vomiting, generalised weakness, and abdominal cramps. No blood in stools. No recent travel.
Past History: Hypothyroidism (2 years).
Examination: Temp 99.8°F | Pulse 112 bpm | BP 100/70 mmHg | RR 20/min | SpO₂ 98%.
Investigations: CBC — mild leukocytosis. Serum Electrolytes — hyponatremia. Stool — no blood/parasites. RFT — mildly elevated creatinine due to dehydration.

Output:
Michael Smith, a 32-year-old man, was admitted on 02/03/2026 and discharged on 05/03/2026. He came with 3 days of loose motions (watery diarrhea), vomiting, stomach cramps, and weakness. He has had hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) for 2 years. On arrival, his temperature was 99.8°F (mild fever), pulse was 112 bpm (fast heart rate; normal is 60–100), blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg (borderline low; normal is 120/80), respiratory rate was 20/min, and oxygen was normal at 98%. Blood tests showed leukocytosis (mild rise in infection-fighting cells) and hyponatremia (low salt/sodium levels due to fluid loss). Stool tests showed no blood or parasites. Kidney tests showed mildly raised creatinine due to dehydration (lack of fluids). He was treated with IV fluids and supportive medicines, improved well, and was safely discharged home.

--- Example 2 ---
Original Medical Report:
Patient Name: Robert Brown | Age/Sex: 58/M | Admission: 25/03/2026 | Discharge: 30/03/2026
C/O: Chest pain and sweating for 6 hours.
History: Sudden onset retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left arm, sweating, mild breathlessness.
Past History: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (8 years). Hypertension (10 years). Dyslipidemia.
Examination: Temp 98.4°F | Pulse 96 bpm | BP 160/100 mmHg | RR 22/min | SpO₂ 95%.
Investigations: ECG — ST depression in anterior leads. Troponin-I — elevated. 2D Echo — mild left ventricular dysfunction. Lipid Profile — elevated LDL cholesterol.

Output:
Robert Brown, a 58-year-old man, was admitted on 25/03/2026 and discharged on 30/03/2026. He has an 8-year history of diabetes (sugar), 10-year hypertension (high BP), and dyslipidemia (high blood cholesterol). He arrived with 6 hours of sudden central chest pain spreading to his left arm, sweating, and mild breathlessness. His temperature was 98.4°F (normal), pulse was 96 bpm, blood pressure was high at 160/100 mmHg (normal 120/80), and oxygen saturation was 95% (borderline). An ECG and elevated troponin-I (a heart damage marker) confirmed a mild heart attack. A 2D Echo (heart ultrasound scan) showed mild left ventricular dysfunction (mild pumping weakness of the heart), and tests showed elevated bad LDL cholesterol. He was stabilized on heart medications and blood thinners, recovered safely, and was discharged home.

You were admitted on 11/08/2020 because the dressing of the Schilley catheter (tube placed in a vein) in the right femoral vein (groin vein) was leaking and you had severe left lower back pain that started three days earlier, along with weakness (asthenia) and difficulty walking. You did not have fever, nausea, vomiting or any other symptoms, and the person who came with you said the same.

During the hospital stay, doctors found several serious infections. A blood test showed a bloodstream infection (infection in the blood) caused by Staphylococcus aureus MRSA (a type of “super‑bug”). The same bug was also found on the catheter tip on 11/08. Because of this, the catheter was removed on 11/08 and you started an antibiotic called vancomycin (a medicine that fights serious bacterial infections) on the same day, guided by the lab results. Your blood cultures became negative after a few days and you stayed without fever (afebrile) for the rest of the stay.

Imaging of your spine showed pyogenic spondylodiscitis (bone infection) at the L3‑L4 levels, which explained the low back pain and the trouble walking. A CT scan (special X‑ray) on 11/12 showed a fracture of the L1 vertebral body (spine bone) because the bone was weak, and gas pockets in the spinal canal at L2‑L3 that could be from a slipped disc (extruded disc herniation) with wear‑and‑tear changes (degenerative disc disease). An MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) on 25/11/2020 confirmed infectious spondylodiscitis with an anterior epidural abscess (pus collection in front of the spinal cord). Another MRI of the pelvis on 25/10/2020 showed a left ileopsoas abscess (pus collection in a deep muscle of the abdomen) measuring 15 × 2.1 × 1.8 cm with swelling (edema) and contrast enhancement. A percutaneous drainage attempt (needle drainage through the skin) on 12/02 was not done because loops of bowel were in the way, as noted by {organization}.

An echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart) done on 11/18 revealed bacterial endocarditis (infection of the heart lining) with a vegetation (small growth) on the mitral valve (one of the heart’s doors). This was also linked to the same Staphylococcus aureus infection.

Because you could not move much, you developed a sacral pressure injury (bed sore on the lower back). This was treated with surgical debridement (removal of dead tissue) and local wound care, and the wound‑care instructions were given to you.

You also needed regular hemodialysis (machine that cleans the blood) on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays because of an arteriovenous fistula (a surgically created connection in the left upper arm to help dialysis). The fistula showed narrowing (stenosis) that will be evaluated later with a vein X‑ray (phlebography) and possibly an ultrasound.

At discharge on 01/02/2021, after a stay of 1 month 24 days 15 hours, you were in good general condition: you looked a little pale (about one‑quarter pale), were hydrated, had normal skin colour (acyanic, anicteric), no fever to the touch, and breathed comfortably in room air. You were awake, aware of time, place and person. Your lungs made normal breath sounds with a few faint crackles at the bases but no breathing trouble. Your heart rhythm was irregular but the sounds were normal and there were no murmurs. Your abdomen was slightly swollen but soft, with normal bowel sounds, normal blood pressure (normotensive), and no pain on pressing. Your arms were warm with good blood flow; the left arm showed a palpable thrill (vibration) over the fistula. Your legs had mild swelling and a yellowish skin change on the front of the lower leg (anterior tibial ochre dermatitis).

The lab results during the stay were: catheter tip culture on 11/08 showed vancomycin‑sensitive Staphylococcus aureus; blood cultures on 11/08, 11/11, 11/21, 11/24 showed Staphylococcus aureus (some resistant to oxacillin) and one sample with Citrobacter koseri; a culture on 11/28 was negative, as were cultures on 12/01 and 12/02.

The plan after discharge includes giving 0.5 g of vancomycin after each scheduled hemodialysis session, continuing the antibiotic until 01/09/2021, which will be six weeks after the last negative blood culture. You will have a phlebography (vein X‑ray) of the arteriovenous fistula to locate the narrowing and decide on further treatment; this may be done with ultrasound guidance in the dialysis room. You are on the waiting list for this test, and {organization} will contact you to arrange it.

You have several follow‑up appointments: an outpatient visit on 16/01/2021 to check the sacral pressure injury and receive home‑care instructions; a cardiology outpatient visit for amyloidosis (protein deposit disease of the heart) investigation on 01/13; a motor‑rehabilitation appointment that was missed on 09/09 and is now scheduled for 01/13; and a physiatry (rehab medicine) appointment requested on 12/27. You should also review the pelvic MRI report from 12/16. Your previous chronic medicines will be continued, and you will keep attending dialysis on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

Please keep the transportation arrangement (stretcher taxi) {omitted} for your trips to the dialysis unit, and follow all the wound‑care and medication instructions given by the team.

You were admitted to the hospital on 11/08/2020 and discharged on 01/02/2021, staying for 1 month, 24 days, and 15 hours. You came in with severe pain in your lower left back that started three days before, along with weakness (asthenia) and difficulty walking (altered gait). The person with you said you did not have fever, nausea, or vomiting. There was some discharge from the dressing of your catheter (a tube placed in your body) in your right thigh vein (femoral vein).

During your hospital stay, it was found that you had a bloodstream infection (infection in your blood) caused by a bacteria called Staphylococcus aureus MRSA. This infection led to several other problems:
1.  A bloodstream infection linked to the Schilley catheter (a type of tube) in your right thigh vein.
2.  Bacterial endocarditis (an infection of the inner lining of your heart), specifically affecting your mitral valve (one of the heart valves). An echocardiogram (a heart ultrasound) on 11/18 showed a "vegetation" (a growth caused by infection) on this valve.
3.  Pyogenic spondylodiscitis (an infection of the spinal bones and the discs between them) in your L3/L4 area (lower back). On 11/05, you had low back pain and difficulty walking. A CT scan (a special X-ray) of your lower back on 11/12 showed signs of a possible fracture (break) in your L1 spinal bone due to weak bones, and gas in your spinal canal at L2/L3, which might be from a slipped disc. An infection or inflammation could not be ruled out. A lumbar MRI (a detailed scan of your lower back) on 25/11/2020 confirmed infectious spondylodiscitis with an anterior epidural abscess (a collection of pus in front of your spinal cord).
4.  A left ileopsoas abscess (a collection of pus in a muscle in your abdomen/hip area). An MRI on 25/10/2020 showed a collection of pus in your left ileopsoas muscle, measuring 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm, with swelling (edema) around it.

The catheter was removed on 11/08, and you were started on antibiotic medicine called Vancomycin, based on culture reports (tests to identify bacteria). An attempt was made on 12/02 by the {organization} to drain the pus from the psoas abscess using a needle (percutaneous drainage), but it could not be done because your intestines were in the way.

You showed improvement in the infection in your spine (axial lesions) with the treatment, and the doctors continued with medicines to treat the infections found during your stay. You did not have a fever, and your blood cultures (tests for infection in blood) repeatedly came back negative.

Because you were not moving much, you developed a sacral pressure injury (a bedsore on your lower back). This was treated with surgical debridement (cleaning the wound by removing dead tissue) and other local treatments. The team gave you instructions on how to care for this injury at home.

You also needed hemodialysis (a machine that filters your blood when your kidneys don't work well) on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. This was done through an arteriovenous fistula (a surgically created connection between an artery and a vein) in your left arm, but there was some narrowing (stenosis) in it. You are currently on this kidney treatment.

When you were discharged, your general condition was good. You were a bit pale, hydrated (had enough fluids), not blue (acyanotic), not jaundiced (anicteric), did not have a fever, and were breathing normally (eupneic) in room air.
Neurology: You were conscious and knew the time, place, and who you were.
Respiratory: Your lungs sounded clear on both sides, with some minor crackling sounds at the bottom, but no signs of breathing difficulty.
Cardiac: Your heart rhythm was irregular, but the heart sounds were normal, with no murmurs (extra heart sounds).
Abdomen: Your stomach was a bit swollen, bowel sounds were present, it was not tense, and not painful when touched lightly or deeply. There were no signs of irritation in the lining of your abdomen.
Your hands and feet were warm and had good blood flow.
Upper limbs: The fistula in your left arm had a good "thrill" (a vibration felt over the fistula, indicating it's working).
Lower limbs: You had some mild swelling (edema) and reddish-brown skin discoloration (ochre dermatitis) on your shins.

Cultures (tests for bacteria) showed:
*   Catheter tip on 11/08: Staphylococcus aureus, sensitive to Vancomycin.
*   Blood culture on 11/08: Staphylococcus aureus.
*   Blood culture on 11/11: Staphylococcus aureus, resistant to Oxacillin (oxa r) in two samples.
*   Blood culture on 11/21: Citrobacter koseri in one sample, Staphylococcus aureus in one sample.
*   Blood culture on 11/24: Staphylococcus capitis.
*   Blood cultures on 11/28, 12/01, and 12/02 were negative.

An MRI of your pelvis was done on 12/16. It was arranged with [organization] for you to attend hemodialysis at [organization] on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, with transport by stretcher taxi from your city.

You are being discharged with the following instructions and pending issues:
*   You need to take 0.5 grams of Vancomycin (an antibiotic) after each scheduled hemodialysis session. This antibiotic treatment will continue until 01/09/2021, completing 6 weeks after your last negative blood culture.
*   Your arteriovenous fistula needs to be checked. A phlebography (a special X-ray of veins) of the fistula is recommended to find the site of narrowing (stenosis). This will help decide if another phlebography or an ultrasound before the procedure is needed. You have been put on a list for this. [organization] will contact you to schedule this treatment.
*   For your sacral pressure injury, the specialist team noted that your follow-up appointment is on 16/01/2021 for reassessment. You were given instructions for home care of the injury.
*   You need cardiology (heart doctor) follow-up to investigate amyloidosis (a condition where abnormal protein builds up in organs). You missed an appointment on 09/09, and a new one is scheduled for 01/13 for motor rehabilitation (physical therapy). We are waiting for an appointment from the physiatry department (physical medicine and rehabilitation) at [organization], which was requested on 12/27.
*   The nuclear magnetic resonance (MRI) report of your pelvis from 12/16 needs to be checked.
*   Your previous long-term medications will be continued.
*   You will go for dialysis on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays.
*   Your cardiology outpatient clinic appointment for amyloidosis is on 01/13.
*   Your pressure injury surgery outpatient clinic appointment is on 01/16.

He came to the hospital for a hemodialysis (blood filtering machine for kidney failure) session with severe left lower back pain that had started 3 days ago, along with weakness and difficulty walking. The person accompanying him said he did not have fever, nausea, or vomiting. The catheter (a tube for dialysis) dressing in his right thigh vein was leaking.

During his hospital stay, he was diagnosed with several serious infections. He had a bloodstream infection (infection in the blood) caused by Staphylococcus aureus MRSA (a type of bacteria resistant to some antibiotics). This infection led to spondylodiscitis (infection of the spinal bones and discs) in his L2-L4 region (lower back), infective endocarditis (infection of the heart valve) in his mitral valve (one of the heart's main valves), and an ileopsoas muscle abscess (a collection of pus in a muscle near the hip) on the left side.

The catheter in his right thigh vein was removed on 11/08, and he was started on antibiotic therapy (treatment with medicines to fight infection) with vancomycin (a strong antibiotic) on the same day, based on culture (lab test to identify bacteria) results. An attempt to drain the abscess in his psoas muscle (a deep muscle in the abdomen) on 12/02 was not successful because bowel loops (parts of the intestine) were in the way.

He showed improvement in the infections in his spine with conservative treatment (treatment without surgery). He remained without fever, and his blood cultures (blood tests for infection) became negative repeatedly. As a complication of being immobile (not moving much), he developed a sacral pressure injury (a bed sore on the lower back), which was treated with surgical debridement (removal of dead tissue) and local care. Instructions for caring for this injury at home were given to the team.

He continued to need hemodialysis on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays because of a problem with his arteriovenous fistula (a surgically created connection between an artery and a vein for dialysis) in his left arm, where there was some narrowing. He is currently on renal replacement therapy (treatment for kidney failure, like dialysis).

His general condition is good. He is a bit pale, hydrated (has enough fluids), not blue (acyanotic), not jaundiced (anicteric), not feverish to the touch, and breathing normally (eupneic) in room air. Neurologically, he is conscious and knows where he is, what time it is, and who he is. When listening to his chest, there were normal breathing sounds with some mild crackles (small popping sounds) at the bottom of both lungs, but no signs of breathing difficulty. His heart rhythm was irregular, with normal heart sounds and no murmurs (abnormal heart sounds). His abdomen (belly) is slightly bulging, with normal bowel sounds, not tense, and not painful when touched lightly or deeply. His hands and feet are warm and have good blood flow. In his left arm, the fistula has a thrill (a vibration felt over the fistula, which is a good sign). In his legs, there is some mild swelling and a skin condition called anterior tibial ochre dermatitis (skin discoloration on the shins).

An MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scan on 25/10/2020 showed a collection of pus in his left ileopsoas muscle, measuring 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm, with swelling and enhancement (brightening on the scan after dye injection).

Culture results showed:
- Catheter tip on 11/08: Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to vancomycin.
- Blood culture on 11/08: Staphylococcus aureus.
- Blood culture on 11/11: Staphylococcus aureus resistant to oxacillin (another antibiotic) in 2 samples.
- Blood culture on 11/21: Citrobacter koseri (another type of bacteria) in 1 sample, and Staphylococcus aureus in 1 sample.
- Blood culture on 11/24: Staphylococcus capitis (another type of bacteria).
- Blood cultures on 11/28, 12/01, and 12/02 were negative.

An attempted puncture to drain the abscess on 12/02 was not done because of intestinal loops being in the way. A new MRI report of the pelvis from 12/16 was reviewed.

It has been arranged with {organization} for him to attend hemodialysis at {organization} on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, with transport by stretcher taxi from his home city.

- For cardiology (heart specialist) follow-up to investigate amyloidosis (a condition where abnormal protein builds up in organs), he missed an appointment on 09/09. A new appointment is scheduled for 01/13.
- For motor rehabilitation (therapy to improve movement), an appointment with the physiatry department (physical medicine and rehabilitation) at {organization} was requested on 12/27, and we are awaiting the appointment.

- His previous chronic medications (long-term medicines) are to be continued.
- He will go to the dialysis room on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays.
- He has an appointment at the amyloidosis cardiology outpatient clinic on 01/13.
- He has an appointment at the pressure injury surgery outpatient clinic on 01/16.

You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

You were admitted on 09/19/2022 and discharged on 10/19/2022 after a stay of 1 month 11 hours in the ward. You are a 60‑year‑old woman, incomplete high‑school education, working as a cleaner, weighing about 60 kg (estimated) and 57 kg (predicted), height 164 cm.  

During this admission you had several serious problems: a resolved septic shock (dangerous infection causing very low blood pressure) with a pulmonary focus (lung infection), acute respiratory failure (severe breathing difficulty), hypotension (low BP), decreased level of consciousness (drowsy), a blood culture that grew staphylococcus aureus (type of bacteria) resistant to oxacillin (antibiotic), a coronavirus infection in March confirmed by RTPCR on 03/15, acute kidney injury (kidney damage) KDIGO 1 that resolved and was pre‑renal (due to low blood flow), and liver cirrhosis (scarring of the liver) with pleural effusion (fluid around the lung) that needed repeated thoracentesis (draining fluid from the chest) and paracentesis (draining fluid from the abdomen).  

On 09/19 a blood gas showed a pH of 7.378, albumin 0.49 g/dL, serum albumin 2.1 g/dL, glucose 164 mg/dL, LDH 72 U/L, and a thoracentesis yielded transudate (fluid low in protein) with protein 2 g/dL, serum protein 7.7 g/dL, LDH 72 U/L, serum LDH 279 U/L, pH 7.378, albumin 0.61 g/dL, serum albumin 1.9 g/dL, amylase 117 U/L, glucose 183 mg/dL and a gram‑stain negative culture. On 09/23 you had 700 mL of transudate drained, on 10/06 1000 mL, on 10/10 another 1000 mL and on 10/15 a further 1000 mL were removed.  

Your liver cirrhosis aetiology (cause) is still to be clarified in a follow‑up gastroclinic appointment. On 02/09/2022 you were advised to increase furosemide (diuretic that removes fluid) to 40 mg twice daily and spironolactone (potassium‑sparing diuretic) to 50 mg daily because of massive ascites (abdominal fluid), dyspnea (shortness of breath) and weight gain. A paracentesis that day removed 4.1 L of ascitic fluid, and another on 13/09 removed 1.4 L.  

You were referred from the emergency unit with a report of admission on 18/09/2022, 85 % room‑air oxygen saturation, obtunded (very sleepy), peripheral cyanosis (bluish skin) and livedo reticularis (mottled skin), and you were intubated (tube placed in the airway) without complications. Four ampoules of furosemide were given before transport but no urine was produced. You were admitted intubated, sedated with midazolam (calm‑inducing drug) and fentanyl (painkiller), paralyzed with rocuronium (muscle relaxant), and supported with norepinephrine (drug to raise BP) at 20 mL/h.  

Initially you were thought to have acute respiratory failure due to coronavirus, congestion or sepsis of pulmonary focus. Empirical ceftriaxone (antibiotic) was started and a diagnostic paracentesis showed no spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (infection of abdominal fluid). On the same day a thoracentesis removed 1000 mL of transudate and a relief paracentesis removed 4000 mL; albumin (protein given intravenously) was given because of the large fluid removal. A point‑of‑care ultrasound on 09/19 showed lung lines and pleural thickening, supporting the lung infection hypothesis.  

Because the blood culture grew staphylococcus aureus, clarithromycin (antibiotic) and clindamycin (antibiotic) were added on 09/24, and the regimen was changed from ceftriaxone + clarithromycin to levofloxacin (antibiotic) + oxacillin (antibiotic) as directed by the consulting team. An echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) was ordered to look for endocarditis (infection of the heart lining). On the morning of 09/27, antibiotics were escalated to meropenem (broad‑spectrum antibiotic) + oxacillin because CRP (inflammation marker) rose and more vasoactive drugs were needed.  

Your breathing improved, you were taken off the ventilator (extubated) on 10/03 and stopped supplemental oxygen on 10/13. The septic condition resolved and the antibiotic course finished on 10/08. You remained in hospital for 24‑hour nursing care, pressure‑injury (skin sore) management, oxygen therapy, and ongoing control of ascites and pleural effusion, as you had no social support for discharge.  

Your past liver history includes first diagnosis of cirrhosis with unclear cause, Child‑B7 MELD 9 (liver severity scores), biopsies in 07/2020 showing grade I fibrosis (early scarring) and in 2021 showing intense fibrosis with moderate steatosis (fatty liver) consistent with grade 2 steatohepatitis stage 3. Complications have been ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, and esophageal varices (enlarged veins in the esophagus) without recent bleeding.  

Other past conditions: diabetes mellitus (sugar disease) diagnosed 15 years ago, systemic arterial hypertension (high BP) for 10 years, non‑toxic multinodular goiter (enlarged thyroid) diagnosed 201

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). 9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.

She has a history of liver cirrhosis (scarring of the liver), diabetes (sugar), high BP, and anxiety/depression. She was admitted for septic shock (severe body-wide infection causing low BP), acute respiratory failure (breathing difficulty), and low consciousness. Blood tests found Staphylococcus aureus (a type of bacteria) and a prior coronavirus infection. She also had acute kidney injury (kidney stress) and fluid buildup in her belly (ascites) and chest (pleural effusion).

During her stay, she was intubated (breathing tube inserted) and sedated. Doctors performed paracentesis (draining belly fluid) and thoracentesis (draining chest fluid) multiple times to relieve pressure. Antibiotics were adjusted based on test results, including Ceftriaxone, Clarithromycin, Levofloxacin, Oxacillin, and Meropenem, to fight the infection. Her breathing improved, and the tube was removed on 10/03. She stayed in the hospital for nursing care, pressure injury treatment, and fluid management because she lacked social support at home.

Before admission, she took Insulin NPH and Glifage XR for sugar, Losartan and Hydrochlorothiazide for BP, Simvastatin for cholesterol, Sertraline and Amitriptyline for mood, Gabapentin for pain, Propranolol for heart protection, Omeprazole for stomach acid, and Furosemide/Spironolactone to reduce fluid. Her family was informed of her serious condition, and they decided together not to perform new invasive procedures. She was discharged with instructions to adjust diuretic doses, monitor kidney function, and continue fluid drainage as needed.

[person] was admitted to the hospital on 09/19/2022 and discharged on 10/19/2022, staying for 1 month and 11 hours in a ward. She is a 60-year-old female cleaner from [address] with incomplete high school education. Her estimated weight is 60 kg, predicted weight 57 kg, and height 164 cm. She has liver cirrhosis (scarring of the liver). During this stay, she had septic shock (severe infection causing low BP) from a lung source, acute respiratory failure (breathing difficulty), low BP, and decreased consciousness. Blood tests showed Staphylococcus aureus bacteria. She also had acute kidney injury (kidney stress) which resolved. Her liver condition caused pleural effusion (fluid around lungs) and ascites (fluid in belly), requiring paracentesis (draining belly fluid) and thoracentesis (draining lung fluid).

On 09/19, belly fluid tests showed low protein and albumin. Lung fluid tests showed it was a transudate (fluid from pressure, not infection). On 09/23, 700 ml of lung fluid was drained. On 10/06, 1000 ml was drained. On 10/10, 1000 ml was drained. On 10/15, 1000 ml was drained. Before this admission, she was seen on 02/09/2022 for massive ascites and breathing trouble. Her diuretics (water pills) were increased to Furosemide 40 mg twice daily and Spironolactone 50 mg daily. Paracentesis drained 4.1 liters that day. On 13/09, another paracentesis drained 1.4 liters. She was referred from emergency care on 18/09/2022 with low oxygen levels, confusion, and blue skin. She was intubated (breathing tube inserted) and sedated.

In the hospital, she was treated for possible lung infection or sepsis. Ceftriaxone (antibiotic) was started. Tests ruled out belly infection. Lung fluid was drained. A POCUS (quick ultrasound) showed lung lines and thickening, supporting sepsis. On 09/24, antibiotics changed to Levofloxacin and Oxacillin after blood cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus. An echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) was done to check for heart valve infection. On 09/27, antibiotics were escalated to Meropenem and Oxacillin due to worsening inflammation. She improved, was removed from the breathing tube on 10/03, and stopped oxygen on 10/13. Antibiotics ended on 10/08. She stayed longer for nursing care, pressure injury treatment, and fluid management.

Her history includes liver cirrhosis diagnosed in 2021, diabetes, high BP, and anxiety. She has had previous biopsies showing liver fibrosis and fatty liver. She has esophageal varices (swollen veins in food pipe). She is allergic to Dipyrone. She used to smoke and drink beer but stopped. Her home medicines include Insulin, Glifage XR (for sugar), Simvastatin (for cholesterol), Losartan (for BP), Hydrochlorothiazide (water pill), Sertraline (for mood), Gabapentin (for nerve pain), Calcium/Vitamin D, Amitriptyline (for pain/sleep), Propranolol (for BP/varices), Omeprazole (for stomach acid), Furosemide, and Spironolactone.

During the stay, she had a nasoenteral tube (feeding tube), central venous access (IV line in neck), and urinary catheter (urine tube). Blood cultures showed Staphylococcus aureus initially, then other harmless bacteria. Lung and belly fluid cultures were negative. A CT scan showed lung fluid and heart enlargement. The heart ultrasound showed normal pumping strength but some valve leakage.

At discharge, her diuretic doses will be adjusted while monitoring kidneys. She will continue to have belly and lung fluid drained as needed. Oxygen support will be reduced slowly. The feeding tube will be removed if she eats well. Pressure sores on her back and hips will be treated. She has a follow-up appointment on 18/01. The family has been informed about the seriousness of her condition. A decision was made together not to perform new invasive procedures.

Rules:

2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.

9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.

You are a 60-year-old woman with liver cirrhosis (severe scarring of the liver). You were admitted on 09/19/2022 and discharged on 10/19/2022, staying for 1 month and 11 hours.

You were admitted from the emergency unit on 09/18/2022 because you had low oxygen levels (85% room air desaturation), were confused (obtunded), had bluish skin (peripheral cyanosis), and a mottled skin pattern (livedo reticularis). You were immediately put on a breathing tube (orotracheal intubation) without any problems. You had been feeling breathless since that morning. Before admission, you were given 4 injections of furosemide (a water pill) but did not pass any urine.

When you were admitted, you were on a breathing tube, sedated (given medicines to make you sleep) with midazolam and fentanyl, and given rocuronium (a muscle relaxant). Your blood pressure was stable with norepinephrine (a medicine to raise BP).

During your hospital stay, doctors thought you had acute respiratory failure (sudden lung failure) due to coronavirus, fluid buildup in the lungs (congestion), or a severe infection (sepsis) in your lungs. You had a coronavirus infection in March, confirmed by an RTPCR test on 03/15.

You were started on ceftriaxone (an antibiotic to fight infection). A paracentesis (procedure to drain fluid from the abdomen) was done, and there were no signs of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (an infection of the abdominal fluid). On the same day, a thoracentesis (procedure to drain fluid from around the lungs) was done, removing 1000 ml of fluid, which was a transudate (a type of fluid buildup). Another paracentesis was done, removing 4000 ml of fluid, and you were given albumin (a protein) because of the large fluid removal.

On 09/19, an ultrasound (POCUS) showed lines and thickening around your lungs, which, along with your breathing failure and need for BP-raising medicines, strongly suggested a lung infection (sepsis of pulmonary focus) as the cause of your breathing problems. So, clarithromycin and clindamycin (more antibiotics) were added.

On 09/24, after blood cultures (tests for infection in blood) showed growth of Staphylococcus aureus (a type of bacteria), your antibiotics were changed from ceftriaxone and clarithromycin to levofloxacin and oxacillin, as advised by [organization]. On the same day, an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound) was requested to check for endocarditis (infection of the heart valves) because of the bacteria found in your blood.

On 09/27 morning, your antibiotics were changed again to meropenem and oxacillin because your CRP (a marker of inflammation) worsened, and you needed more BP-raising medicines.

You slowly improved with your breathing and were taken off the breathing tube (extubation) on 10/03. Supplemental oxygen was stopped on 10/13. Your infection (septic condition) resolved, and you completed your antibiotic course on 10/08.

You remained in the hospital because you needed 24-hour nursing care, treatment for pressure injuries (bedsores), oxygen therapy, and management of ascites (fluid in the abdomen) and pleural effusion (fluid around the lungs). You did not have social support to go home.

You have a history of liver cirrhosis, first diagnosed in 2019, with the cause still being investigated. You have had complications like ascites, shp (hepatopulmonary syndrome, a lung problem due to liver disease) with medium-sized varices (swollen veins), spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, eh (hepatic encephalopathy, brain dysfunction due to liver disease), and upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

You also have a history of diabetes (sugar) for 15 years, hypertension (high BP) for 10 years, and a non-toxic multinodular goiter (swelling in the thyroid gland) diagnosed in 2019. You have anxiety and depression, diagnosed 6 years ago, and spondyloarthrosis (arthritis of the spine) with low back pain. You have a painful lump in your right breast, which was biopsied in November 2019 and was likely a fibroadenoma (a non-cancerous lump).

You used to smoke one pack a day for a few months and drank 3-4 cans of beer on weekends but stopped 2 years ago. You deny using illicit drugs.

Before this hospitalization, you were taking several medications: Insulin NPH (for sugar), Glifage XR 500 mg (for sugar), Simvastatin 20 mg/day (for cholesterol), Losartan 50 mg (for BP), Hydrochlorothiazide (a water pill), Sertraline 50 mg (for depression), Gabapentin 300 mg/day (for nerve pain), Calcium and vitamin D, Amitriptyline 25 mg (for depression/nerve pain), Propranolol 10 mg (for BP and varices), Omeprazole 40 mg (for acidity), Furosemide 40 mg twice a day (a water pill), and Spironolactone 50 mg/d (a water pill).

On 02/09/2022, you had a consultation where your furosemide was increased to 40 mg twice daily and spironolactone to 50 mg/d due to massive ascites (a lot of fluid in the abdomen), dyspnea (breathlessness), and weight gain. A paracentesis was done, draining 4.1 liters of fluid. Another paracentesis was done on 09/13, draining 1.4 liters.

During this admission, you had several thoracentesis procedures: on 09/19, 09/23 (drained 700 ml), 10/06 (drained 1000 ml), 10/10 (drained 1000 ml), and 10/15 (drained 1000 ml). The fluid was a transudate, and cultures were negative.

Blood cultures showed Staphylococcus aureus on 09/19, Staphylococcus epidermidis on 09/24, and Staphylococcus capitis on 09/28. All were resistant to oxacillin. Urine, pleural fluid, ascitic fluid, and catheter tip cultures were negative.

A CT scan on 09/21 showed bilateral pulmonary opacities (shadows in both lungs) that could be fluid or inflammation, bilateral pleural effusion (fluid around both lungs) with atelectasis (collapsed lung areas) in the lower parts, and cardiomegaly (enlarged heart). An echocardiogram showed a normal ejection fraction (heart's pumping strength) of 59%, a dilated left atrium (upper heart chamber), preserved ventricular systolic performance (normal squeezing of the main pumping chambers), normal heart wall movement, mild mitral and tricuspid valve insufficiency (mild leakage of heart valves), and mild left ventricular diastolic dysfunction (mild problem with heart relaxing).

Your plan for discharge includes adjusting your water pill doses, closely watching your kidney function, continuing relief paracentesis and thoracentesis as needed, gradually reducing oxygen therapy, assessing if the feeding tube (nasoenteric tube) can be removed if you eat well by mouth, and caring for your pressure injuries on your back and hips. You have a follow-up appointment at AGAF on 01/18. Your family has been informed about the seriousness of your condition and the possible outcomes, and a shared decision was made not to perform any new invasive procedures.
